Final Fantasy XV is a gaming journey for both new comers to the series as for old fans. It's not merely a game; it's an odyssey, a breathtaking journey through a meticulously crafted world that deserves to be savored slowly, like a fine aged wine. This is not just a game; it's an unforgettable adventure that invites players to immerse themselves fully and embrace every moment even if at times is not perfect and without its issues.

The Art of the Journey:
Final Fantasy XV is not a mere collection of quests and battles; it's an artful exploration of a fantastical world called Eos. The game's meticulous attention to detail is staggering, from the sprawling cities and lush landscapes to the smallest character nuances. Every location, every character, every creature feels like it has a purpose and a story to tell. Playing this game at a measured pace allows you to truly absorb and appreciate the sheer depth of this world not to say the fact e very food you cook has a detailed model that always made me hungry >.< if there is a lacking of the game world is that is not interactive as its detailed and beautiful.

A Story Worth Savoring:
The heart of Final Fantasy XV lies in its rich narrative. The story of Prince Noctis and his loyal companions is a sweeping epic filled with emotions, betrayals, and moments of camaraderie. It's a tale of growth and self-discovery, where the characters evolve alongside the player. To rush through it would be like flipping through the pages of a novel, missing the intricacies of character development and the emotional resonance that slowly builds over time.

The Beauty of Exploration:
Eos is a vast and diverse world, and the true joy of the game comes from exploring its nooks and crannies. The open-world design invites players to wander, discover hidden treasures, engage with locals, and undertake side quests that breathe life into the world. Taking your time allows you to fully embrace the wonder of the journey, to find hidden caves, secret fishing spots, and breathtaking vistas that you might otherwise overlook.

A Symphony of Combat and Strategy:
Final Fantasy XV's combat system is a symphony of strategy and finesse. Engaging in real-time battles requires careful planning and coordination with your companions. Rushing into fights may lead to missed opportunities for tactical brilliance and inventive strategies. Taking your time to master the intricacies of combat can be immensely rewarding and showcases the true depth of the game's mechanics.

The Slow Burn of Character Development:
One of the most beautiful aspects of Final Fantasy XV is watching the characters grow. The subtle changes in their personalities, their relationships, and their bonds with Noctis are best appreciated when the game is played at a thoughtful pace. Rushing through would mean missing out on the gradual transformation of these characters from acquaintances to lifelong friends.

Conclusion:
Final Fantasy XV isn't just a game; it's a poignant journey that deserves to be experienced at a slow, deliberate pace. It's an emotional rollercoaster, a visual feast, and a testament to the power of storytelling in gaming. So, fellow adventurer, take your time, breathe in the world of Eos, savor every story beat, and explore every corner. Final Fantasy XV is a masterpiece for some and a terrible game or final fantasy for others and that ok but still deserves a proper go to try yourself, and like all great art, it's meant to be savored slowly, one spellbinding moment at a time.

Configuration tips:
1) Turning off all NVIDIA extra graphics settings improves FPS by a ton. Hairworks is the most lightweight one though (costs about 2fps) and looks amazing so I kept that one on.

2) The High-Resolution Pack works great on a GTX 1070 (on 1440p res), even though it lists minimum requirements as being a GTX 1080 Ti, and I recommend you get it if you run a resolution greater than 1080p, have a GPU with 8GBs of VRAM, and have the extra 65GBs of space for it.

3) If you have performance issues remember to update your drivers. Both Nvidia and AMD have new drivers that include optimization for this game.

4) IMPORTANT EDIT: I originally had a guide here on how to edit the .ini file to support a 144hz monitor. After playing a little longer I noticed some bugs I was having such as long black screens before loading and hunt posters staying on screen after turning the quests in. Turns out this was due to editing the .ini file. Please reset your .ini file if you are having issues after editing it from my guide or another. Edits other than framerate can cause similar issues too. I recommend leaving the file alone for now.

5) The options you get when booting up the game "Television" or "Home Theater" don't affect your display, they actually affect your audio. It also had nothing to do with stereo or surround sound. It determines audio compression. If you are using low quality speakers select "Television" as it will sound better for you. Otherwise choose "Home Theater".

Note: I know many are reporting random CTDs or frame drops but I haven't experienced a single CTD and the game runs smooth as butter for me staying between 50-60 fps even when encountering large enemies (i7-4790k, GTX 1070, 16GB 2133 DDR3 RAM, SSD).

Final Fantasy XV is a beautiful game. That's a corny way to start off a review, but I want to get out with it. I know it had a long and troubled production, and that it came out unfinished, and it rubbed a lot of fans the wrong way. I remember reading forum discussions in 2013 where players would ask, "Do companies think it's right to make us wait ten years for a game?"

Well, if they put stuff out on par with this game, they absolutely can. I'll get on with my life in the meanwhile. I'm a bit more sympathetic to those who played it on release. But I can't really know or care much about how the game was seven years ago, so much as what it was like when I was playing it seven days ago.

It tells the tale of four friends who set out on a journey to obtain a ring and end up fighting a threat that could plunge the world in darkness forevermore (J. R. R. Tolkien should sue). Prince Noctis and his childhood friends-turned-bodyguards are planning to have the best road trip ever before he gets married and saves the world and all that. These lads are a Japanese schoolgirl's wet dream - carelessly handsome, unabashedly silly, and more concerned with the trendiness of their clothes than the gravitas of their duties.

This is the highlight of Final Fantasy XV - the main cast is a bunch of sheltered dandies who have to come to terms with the greatness that has been thrust upon them. Their personal growth, their earnest moments of brotherhood, and their banter-laden interactions are the heart of the narrative. The hero isn't a po-faced paladin of justice - he's one of the guys. Watching him mature into a true king is quite the journey.

Final Fantasy XV also has one of the most beautifully rendered open worlds I've seen. It caused me to appreciate nature more, because real life looks a lot like Final Fantasy XV. And trust me, you spend about as much time driving in this game as you would in real life. The car, the Regalia, is the fifth main character. If there's one thing I could wish for, it would be that your control over the car wasn't so limited for most of the game. But even with its mostly autopilot navigation, sitting back and admiring the scenery while listening to music from past FF titles was quite the experience.

This open-world design continues for half the game, of which most of your time will be spent doing sidequests. I'm told I generally rush RPGs, but I definitely didn't rush Final Fantasy XV, because there's so much to do - and so much fun to be had doing it. It's enough to put the main story on the backburner, it is, what with all the games-within-a-game it offers. Fishing? Monster hunting? Pinball on steroids? This game has it. And with the game's reward mechanics, plus the promise of interesting conversations with the supporting cast, nearly every sidequest feels worth doing. Even if it's a blatant advertisement for Cup Noodles. Look, they had to get the budget to make this game look so beautiful somewhere, okay?

In an inversion of Final Fantasy XIII, the first half of XV is open-world and laden with sidequests, while the second half is linear. I know 'linearity' is a dirty word to a lot of gamers, but I can't complain about it in either of these games. Once the plot in Final Fantasy XV starts getting funneled towards its conclusion, it also becomes much more focused and much more heartrending. I was almost in tears in this game's campaign as I've been with all the previous games I've played put together. And I commend the game's writing and directing team for being unafraid to commit to the tragedy, something quite a few Final Fantasy stories pull back from at the last moment. For its story alone, Final Fantasy XV is a triumph.

This game also marks a true departure from the Active Time Battle system of past Final Fantasies, something the series has been trying to break away from for over a decade. Finally, the series commits to real-time hack-and-slash combat. There's a wait mode, but it seems to simply be an accessibility option for handicapped players. The combat is a lot of fun. Once you get the hang of the dodge/parry mechanics, and can switch between defense and aggression on the fly, there's a lot of fun to be had, even if the camera sometimes obstructs your view when fighting large enemies.

While I encountered no major bugs during my playthrough, there is no hiding the fact that this is very much a game that spent ten years in development. Final Fantasy XV is hardly consistent, but then again, the Final Fantasy series as a whole isn't consistent. My favourite analogy to make is that if Dragon Quest is AC/DC, Final Fantasy is Guns N' Roses. It's large, unwieldy and all over the place, but if it's a series of very low lows (FF XIII-2), it also has very high highs. Final Fantasy XV is a very high high. If Metal Gear Solid V hadn't come out, on release XV would have been the greatest unfinished game ever made. But it is finished now, with DLC episodes to fill in the blanks and show how adaptable the game engine is to different gameplay styles, and it goes on sale for a fiver. There is no better time to play this game than now.

Ultimately, Final Fantasy XV is a fantastic experience with a lot to do and even more to appreciate. Its emphasis on brotherhood reminded me of my own college clique. I oughta call those guys sometime.

8.5 out of 10. The game isnt perfect. But one thing always stood out to me: the relationship between the four main characters, every time I camped, every time we talked, every time they would come up with random quips at each other, or compliment each other's combat, it all was very unique for a game. 

But that finale. That finale hit me so hard, from the moment you pick your picture from the ones you saved, to Regi dealing the final blow, the final camp scene all the friends in 1 pic. 
I cried like a baby through it all, I loved every moment of it, I can say that this games journey was worth it, through all the ups and downs the boys were always there, and in the end it's because of their relationship that this game was elevated from being a game that I only wanted to "get over with" to see the story, to one of my favorite stories in recent JRPGs, to the point of wanting to find stories like it.
Realization at the ending that this story was actually about the journey. The memories we make in life with those closest to us. And saying goodbye. Is one of the most brilliant pieces I have seen in a long arse time.
I wish, I had friends like that in real life!

[h1]Final Fantasy XV - A Masterpiece?[/h1]

I hadn't played any Final Fantasy games before. I decided to start with Final Fantasy XV after playing the demo, and in my opinion, the game immediately starts off strong.
    
The story grips you right from the start (spoiler alert),[spoiler]beginning with your departure from Insomnia to meet with Luna. However, as always, the journey is not an easy one... In the end of the demo, Noctis's father, Regis, dies, leaving Noctis alone with no family except for his hope in Luna[/spoiler], the demo ends at a very intriguing point, leaving me eager to continue the game and see what happens next. And what follows is even more fascinating. When you buy the game, you'll experience moments that may bring tears, shock, or joy. Overall story rating: [b]10/10[/b]

In terms of gameplay, the controls weren't difficult to manage, but I played with a gamepad because playing with a keyboard is not comfortable at all. The game is challenging to control, so I recommend playing with a gamepad to avoid frustration. It's difficult to execute combos and overall combat can be tough. If you don't have a gamepad, I don't recommend purchasing one, as it could negatively impact your opinion of the gameplay. The in-game tutorial explains everything thoroughly and introduces the game very well. There's no need to grind, unless you want to. I recommend not skipping the tutorial text if you're just starting to get familiar with the game. Overall gameplay rating: [b]9/10[/b]

There are no complaints about the audio. The sound quality is excellent, though it may not be everyone's cup of tea. I can't say it gave me a "wow" effect, but it's simply high-quality audio. The voice acting is top-notch, both in Russian and English (which I used during my playthrough). Overall audio rating:  [b]9/10[/b]
[hr] [b]Additional information for those interested:[/b] the graphics are top-notch, but as a result, the game is very demanding on PC. With an RTX3060 graphics card, Ryzen 3600 processor, and 32GB of RAM, I experienced crashes and freezes. However, according to reviews, this happens rarely—I guess I'm just unlucky. The game is very demanding on high or ultra graphics settings if you want to play with such visual fidelity. There were no bugs that hindered gameplay, except for one additional online collaboration mission where characters stopped in the middle of a mission, but you can exit to the main menu using the interface. The time it takes to complete the game varies for everyone, so it's hard to say exactly how much time it will take. If you only focus on the main story, the game will take about 20-30 hours. The additional episodes take up little time.
[hr] [b]I rate the game a 9/10.[/b] There are few games with such beautiful graphics and an interesting story nowadays. The game was released in 2016 for PS, and in 2018 for PC with improved graphics. Even now, it's still relevant graphically. Few games can boast such audio quality. I hope my recommendation was helpful to you, and with that, I've said all I wanted to about the game!

I honestly don't know what happened behind the scenes, but i refuse to believe this game was made entirely by one team. It feels as if a good, hard working, wonderfully creative team worked on the first half, then something happened, and a lot of people who shouldn't have jobs took over the second half.

The second half is so chalk full of bad writing, massive missed opportunities, poor level design, and a myriad of other problems, that it just makes me so, so incredibly sad. So unfortunately I can't recommend only half a game.

Having played this game on PS4, Xbox Series X and now on PC I must say the "Windows Edition" is the way to play it. If you have yet to play this terrific continuation of the series, I would highly recommend it. Character progression and story are pretty great, and the battle system is addicting - particularly on the higher difficulty levels. 

After having just played FF16, I truly think 15 is more fully realized. I remember when I first started playing the game on PS4 back in the day, I was concerned how they had changed the battle system to a mostly ARPG formula. Even playing it back then I wasn't fully convinced, but playing it in 2023 on a high end PC was eye-opening for me. Once you get the hang of the battle system it is addicting and fun. I found myself seeking out "hunts", where you go kill challenging beasts and raise your rank. This is almost a game in itself, and I spent at least 20 hours on this playthrough running them. The story makes a little more sense to me than 16's did, with everything seeming a little more rooted in the characters and their friendships. This is something I feel many RPGS struggle with. 

On this playthrough I also tried all the "Episodes", which are downloadable several-hour affairs that focus on each of your friends as well as the villain of 15, Ardyn. I think they are actually a very interesting exercise in making the game completely different with each DLC. I actually really liked "Ignis" and "Gladiolus", but prompto was pretty terrible for me. Ardyn I really enjoyed, and I wish in FF16 they had included a similar summoning system. As Ardyn you get to summon Ifrit in battle, and he seems much more a teammate than in the main game of FF15 or even FF16. 

Regardless, if you have been on the fence or if you have never tried a FF before, this game might be a good place to start. Once you get the hang of the battle system it is a fun romp that you can spend anywhere between 50-120 hours on, depending on how much a completionist you are.

[b]Story Spoiler Free Review:[/b]

FFXV is kind of incredible and good at so many things. Unfortunately, being a video game is not one of them. 

I've rarely ever had such complicated feelings about a piece of media. So bear with me as I try to put down all my thoughts about FFXV so my poor wife doesn't have to suffer through this anymore.

I remember when "FFXV" was announced when I was still in high school in 2006. When this game came out in 2016, all I ever heard was how much of a disaster it was to play. I just wrote it off and forgot about it. A while back, it was on sale for not much at all and I figured I would at least see how bad it really was. Or at least I'd watch Kingsglaive to see if it was as sick as the art looked. 

When I started playing this "game", I found this [url=https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2094194252]guide.[/url] Without it, I don't think I would have enjoyed FFXV nearly as much.

I put game in quotes because I realized that to really get at the profoundly broken, yet charming heart of XV you have to re-frame it as a "multimedia experience" as pretentious as that sounds. When you click through the link above, you'll see that there are around 30 steps to fill in the gaps and fully take in the experience. These 30-some disparate parts build a wild, unhinged and fully-fleshed out experience. It's sort of like that Japanese art wherein broken pottery is repaired with gold or silver and it makes it more beautiful overall.

One caveat: I did not try to 100% this game. I did not do many of the side quests. I did them just when I felt like it or needed gil to upgrade/wanted to see other stuff. I stuck to the main story for the most part. I mention this because some of my buds that had played this game said they felt like it was a slog. I didn't feel like that at all, but they also revealed to me that they did try to do everything on the map before moving to the next area. I think this is a recipe for disaster considering how piecemeal a lot of this game is. Which brings me to my next point...

[b]The Bad?[/b]
This game feels like a chaotic mishmash of ideas thrown together without much coherence. The storyline is scattered across various mediums - a movie, an anime, DLC, prequel mobile games that are no longer available - making it hard to follow. Gameplay mechanics such as crafting spells, driving, fishing, cooking, and collecting items feel disjointed. There's even a strange emphasis on upgrading snowmobiles and collecting hats in the DLC and other game systems that will not carry over or have any bearing on anything else. It's just... content for content's sake. Combat and leveling are unbalanced, with over-leveling being too easy. The control scheme is awkward, and the product placement tie-ins and crossover DLC outfits are jarring. Additionally, important character development is lacking until late in the game, leaving me frustrated by the lack of exposition earlier on.

The pacing of this game starts off slow, around a 2, for the first five chapters. Then, it suddenly ramps up to about a 7 for chapters 6-8, and by chapters 9-14, it skyrockets to an intense 11. I am still recovering from the whiplash. Many crucial details that would have enhanced the enjoyment of the entire experience are only revealed in the latter half of the game. I think if the curve had been leveled out and some of the other details given earlier it would have been so much more enjoyable.

It's a shame that the alternate ending/second round of DLCs were scrapped and put into a book. I would have loved to play some of the other characters in the story. 

Once I started to notice these oddities pretty early on, I worried if I would have the stomach to finish this game. I went down a wiki rabbit hole and found one of the most harrowing and fascinating video game production stories I've ever read. [url=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Development_of_Final_Fantasy_XV]I am surprised this game got released at all.[/url] 

[b]The Good:[/b]
Despite all of that bullshit I just said, I really enjoyed my XV experience. I found the characters so charming and they were what kept me coming back. I remember thinking at first that their names were idiotic. However, I slowly fell in love with the final fantasy teenage mutant ninja turtles and was so enamored with their camaraderie/brotherhood that I looked forward to seeing what they would get up to next. I love that they dunk on each other. I love that they support and praise each other. At one point in the game, there is a low point where they are all sort of beefing with one another and it was genuinely heartbreaking to play through. There is another point in the game where Noctis fumbles with his feelings says and finally tells the others over a campfire "You guys... are the best" and I couldn't believe it but it actually kinda fucked me up how much I loved that the boys loved each other.

When you camp at night, Prompto reviews all your photos throughout the day which are just snapshots from his perspective. You get select the ones you want and they are stored in a sort of album building a visual diary of your experience. The boys comment on the photos with sort of generic lines but It always made me so happy when they would say how cool someone looked in a shot, or if you would get a really great candid shot of Iris being adorable or Noctis looking like he really didn't want to have his picture taken in front of a landmark.

They are over-the-top personalities, but their interactions and language makes them feel more real than other characters in not just Final Fantasy but media by a mile. It made me really miss my friends from college that I don't get to see very often.

[b]Final thoughts:[/b]
Final Fantasy XV is an extremely bizarre experience. I've never played anything even remotely like it. I totally understand if you do not like it. However, I believe the boys are too charming to ignore. I'm glad I gave it a shot finally even if I had to use a crazy guide to really get the full experience.

This will never ever happen, but I pray one day someone will recut/re-edit/remaster this game into a tidy package that fixes the pacing and puts all of the media in one place.  I believe this game would finally get the praise it deserves and if that happened, it might be my favorite FF.

This game looks beautiful and promises an open world full of adventure. The graphics are great, and the game runs well, with amazing draw distance and enormous environments. That promise falls apart as soon as you try to explore however. You can not go off the beaten trail more than a few feet before finding an invisible wall or hearing Gladio shouting "Where do you think you're going?" and resetting you to the path. The car is on rails, and as soon as you finally get  control of it, you'll find that it handles worse than Mass Effect 1's Mako. You will constantly see interesting things, like a giant canyon that yearn to be explored, but are forevor off limits and undeveloped beyond just a facade. This is further expounded by the fact that there are no shortcuts. You can't explore or travel straightline from A to B like actual open-world rpgs like Elder Scrolls. Then halfway through It becomes super linear, with a weird tacked on time-travel mechanic to explore the open-world in breaks.

The story (normally a hallmark of Final Fantasy) is banal and unimpressive. All of the characters are underdeveloped and unlikeable. Plot holes abound, with characters switching sides back and forth with no real motivation. The full story could have been played through in under five hours, but the game takes much longer because there is so much nonsensical filler that has no bearing on the characters or story. All the sidequests are uninspired and feel tacked on in order to justify a late in development shift to open world. It feels like SquareEnix saw the success of Witcher 3, and unsuccessfully attempted a "fast follow" without understanding how to execute or the level of redesign needed. [spoiler]Noctis apparently hasn't seen or interacted with his love interest since he was 4, and she sacrifices herself as soon as you see her. There is a slight mention of an extended coma/crystal stasis for years that is never explained. There is an unneccessary and irritating time jump.[/spoiler] The dialogue is just drivel. There is immersion-breaking product placement, including an out-of-place poorly written questline promoting Cup Noodles.

The combat feels like a Janky version of the original Kingdom Heart's system. Pathing is an issue for allies and enemies, which alternatively is irritating and easy to exploit. Equipment progression is uneven. The character stat development is a broken amalgamation of Final Fantasy X and Skyrim's perk system. The dungeons are hours long and tedious with no means to save in them. This, I assume, was to add a level of risk/suspense to them, but the combat and puzzles are undaunting. It just adds tedium as you are running in circles in a repeatedly recycled environment with limited visibility and a useless map trying to find your way to the end and out as quickly as possible. My playtime is not nearly as long as listed. I've literally had to pause the game and leave it running for days, because I wasn't able to finish a dungeon in one session. Multiple times. The summon system, another Final Fantasy hallmark, has become an unreliable mess, with little control or input, and even fewer summons. [spoiler] By the time I got to Leviathan, I was treated to the buildup of what I thought would finally be an epic boss fight with strategy, rellexes and challenge. Instead you just hold attack and litterally watch it die. If you try anything else prepare for nausea as the camera struggles and you have to fight it to target again. This has to be one of the most disappointing moments in gaming for me.[/spoiler]

More insultingly, it has now been abandoned, unfinished, but still for sell at full price.

Remember when this game was first revealed to us like 2 decades ago? Pepperidge Farm remembers :D
[h2] It is important to note that I am approaching this game without the overwhelming rose-tinted nostalgia everyone has for Final Fantasy VII or X. [/h2]

- The story, lorebuilding, characters all pack quite a decent emotional punch, even if the execution is a bit weaker than previous FF titles.
- This is NOT a turn-based or ATB-based game, it's simply real-time action combat. It's a very uncommon model for this franchise, but one that I enjoyed nevertheless.
- Teleporting all over the place is badass as fuck.
- The combos you can do with your boys are flashy as hell and very well-animated, making teamwork very fun. This even includes the temporary story party members too.
- This is a weirdly VERY SIMPLE combat model to grasp. Most of it is hold X to block/dodge and hold B to attack automatically. 
- Switching between 4 equippable weapons on the fly is great.
- I really enjoyed the roadtrip aspect given that you can listen to most of the franchise's prior music on the car radio. The banter between the boys was also quite charming.
- If your favourite color is black, you gonna love this world setting cause it offers little else in the way of color lmao.
- Your photographer party member is so good at his role he will autosnap screenshots for you. He has a combat technique called Selfie Shot that does exactly what it implies. This guy takes pictures literally everywhere; in dungeons, poses next to guards of bases, in the middle of combat, in the fucking bathrooms if he can.
Prompto is EXACTLY how you do an overly-expressive or bitchy character without being too annoying, a very refreshing take given my extreme PTSD of Vanille.
- Everyone needs an Ignis in their lives. Everything about this guy is just *Chef's Kiss*, pun intended. His cooking is pretty fleshed-out and can learn an entire restaurant's worth of recipes, including some absurdly strong endgame party buffs.
- And then there's your musclehead gigachad, Gladio. He is actually the most fun to play with, as he has a skill-based parry with his shield and under the right conditions, can dish out more damage than even the king himself ironically.
- After drinking most of the lore and side content, I connected with and loved this world and a lot of these characters more than most other Final Fantasy games prior, it was kinda refreshing seeing relatable childhood stuff after all the "Super broody, zero emotional depth soldiers" that were Cloud, Squall and Lightning. 
perhaps this is just my male bias but there's just something very endearing about the extreme bromance and unwavering loyalty.
- There are plenty of alternate outfits for all of the bros.
- FINALLY, a final fantasy game that delivers summons in the absolute holy spectacle that they should be.
- FINALLY, a final fantasy game where you can fight enemies in midair for sheer cinema like in the movies.
- Impeccably beautiful top-tier soundtrack as always.
- The Leviathan fight is such a spectacular cinematic feast it deserves its own praise.
- It only took 15 mainline games across 30+ years to finally let us customize our chocobos :)
- In case you weren't invested in the roadtrip aspect already, your car can fucking FLY.
- I really enjoyed the fishing in this game once I got the hang of it.
- There's some pretty fun optional endgame to be found after you finish the story, like the menace dungeons, Melusine, Legendary weapons questchain, even a ported raid boss from FF14 in Garuda.
- The graphics of this game look pretty amazing even after 10+ years.
- EXCELLENT optimization, rock solid 60+ fps on a mid-tier PC, which given the graphical fidelity and the size of this open world, is very impressive.

A royal warning for the following:
- The combat model has much less depth than previous games, where you could spec any party member into any role, be it debuffer, healer, magic dps, etc.
Here it's much more focused on being as flashy as possible instead.
- Introduce main character, introduce his love interest, make them almost never interact with each other, refuse to elaborate, leave. ????????????
It's literally a running meme that Noctis has more chemistry with people in other games where he's a guest appearance than he does with Lunafreya in his own game lmao.
- This is the most fragmented story presentation I've ever seen. If you want to experience all of it (including the basic background introductions to your party members) you need to additionally play 4 separate DLCs, watch a 2-hour movie, a 5-episode anime series, even read a novel. They all really good, don't get me wrong, but all of that should have been in the main game. 
- I really don't like the massive downgrade to the magic system in this game, it's 100% just throwing crafted elemental consumables, where are my healing magics, Esunaga, Hastega, Protectga, Slowga, Deshellga, you know, all the shit we had in previous FF games from like 20 years ago???
Instead the game opts to shower you in potions and elixirs and it becomes Dragon Age Origins PTSD all over again...
- This previous point is doubly frustrating because in the same game there's a multiplayer expansion where you CAN equip and use a bunch of the FF magics with the pretty deep and creative weapon progression system. It's literally like I'm playing a completely different game there.
- 9999 damage limit again? The average vanilla player can break this only with Armiger Unleashed. It feels like a step down having previously played FFXIII, where you could do MILLIONS of damage per second, or even FFXII where you could still do tens of thousands.
- You don't fight half the summons in this game, nor can you really control WHO or WHEN they are summoned either, they just kinda show up randomly when you're in trouble. However, this is fixable with a mod.
- Have you ever heard of a game that contains 67,000+ files???? It's not only over 100 GB in size, but it's extremely slow to copy across drives due to this.
- There are a couple of terribly-designed endgame superbosses that are extremely unfun to fight or take basically forever to kill (or both), like Adamantoise or Omega. It's really annoying for completionists as they are both required for achievements.
- Speaking of achievements, took me around 130 hours to get the 100%...
- The majesty of Liam O'Brien's voice is delegated to the goddamn Innkeeper in Lestallum. The man voiced the main antagonist of the previous games in Caius Ballad for the love of fuck.
- The multiplayer expansion's public matchmaking is dead and has a very nasty difficulty spike around the midgame, which requires reading online guides and seeking the help of the community discord. However, there are still some folks there even after a decade whose assistance did enable me to finish the endgame and enjoy all the content for 40+ hours.

Look, I get it. Game has been in development hell for over a decade, changing name, game director, entire cast, game engine, and lord knows what else. 
Yet despite the odd design choices and shortcomings of this game, there's still that magical grip of an undeniably rich and deep Final Fantasy game, and enough interesting and unique things happening that allow you to endure through it all and let out that long exhale when you roll those final credits listening to "Stand By Me" with all the emotions flowing through and you conclude "Yep, this one's pretty special".

[h1]INTRODUCTION[/h1]
Looks like all those years of people buying Square Enix JRPGs to support the games coming to PC finally paid off. Square Enix finally hit a home run with this game, which they say isn't a port, but a full PC game made from the ground up. It certainly feels like it, and I have to say that it is the most impressive "port" since GTAV. That doesn't mean that it isn't without it's share of bugs, though. Because this game is already a year and a half old, I will only be focusing on the PC related details and all the new content that came with the Royal Edition of the game.

[h1]ROYAL EDITION CONTENT[/h1]
I was one of the people who played this game on launch day for the PS4, back in November 2016, and I must say this game has come a long way since then. Back then there was no offroad Regalia, drivable boat or a great deal of other things. While not exactly Royal Edition content, the ability to accept more than one hunt a time GREATLY enhances gameplay. To those who don't know, back in the day you could only accept one hunt at a time, which meant a lot of coming and going to the same outpost for new missions. Also you could not wait at a campsite to change the time of day. This change alone improves replay value.

I was very impressed with the new story content that they added. It was more than I expected actually. Without spoiling too much, the last chapter of the game used to be a Final Fantasy XIII-style linear corridor with an easy battle and then end credits. Well no more, as the entire last chapter was completely remade into a proper dungeon, loaded with optional side quests and bosses that are quite challenging. The new story content just continues the long mission that Square Enix is on to fill all the plot holes that the launch version of the game created. While it's true that some of this content should have been in the original game since day 1, better late than never, I say. 

My only real complaint about the Royal Edition is the fact that because all of the original DLC is included, you end up with some very OP gear right from the start. With the fishing mini-game, you already have the best rod and reel, making it a breeze compared to the original game. You COULD use the weaker rods for greater challenge, but who is going to do that? Especially since you have to do a lot of fishing to get Noctis's fishing skill up to level 10. And then there is the Magitek Exosuits, which literally make you invincible. They last a long time too, effectively make them a 'win button." Any time you just want to win without a struggle, just suit up. It's morphin' time.

[h1]CONCLUSION[/h1] not COLLUSION! (insert Trump meme)
I managed to get 75 hours out of the PC version of Final Fantasy XV, which is actually my fourth total playthrough of the game. So you can say that I am a big fan. While the PC version does have it's share of bugs, some of which have already been patched out by the time I wrote this, the game was overall quite stable. The game DID crash on me twice in 75 hours, but both times it happened, I was unable to make it happen again at the same spot, leading me to declare them random. Believe it or not, I remember the PS4 launch day version being LESS stable, so this is not bad considering how varied computers can be. We all have different rigs.

With all the new content making it feel like a (finally) complete game and the cheaper price tag, and let's not forget about the upcoming mod support, you TRULY are getting the most superior version of the game. And as a sign of great confidence, they even made available a playable demo, which is becoming more rare every day. I strongly recommend you give this game a shot, as it is welcoming to both fans and newcomers alike.

I won't be doing a score because I consider my review too narrow, focusing just on the stablilty and Royal Edition content.

Tetsuya Nomura’s original vision for what this game was supposed to be (Final Fantasy Versus XIII) would’ve been exactly my type of game. The trailers starting from 2006 were genuinely something else. The mixture of emo / visual kei / Gen X soft club, almost gothic aesthetic, the dark heavy gloomy city atmosphere with the osts of Somnus and Omnis Lacrima playing, the Shakespearean quotes, and then like the implied Romeo and Juliet story/tragedy with the almost Aerith like Stella Nox Fleuret. Noctis's face off against her as they both use their sigils, magic and swords was so cool. Noctis's original fit and personality seemed so badass especially with his Armiger (which is also such a cool reference to Knights of the Round), he seemed to have special red glowing eyes connected to death and was also connected to some dream world hence why he sleeps in the trailers, Stella seemed to have the same power as well that they both kept secret. Then seeing the Emperor face off against King Regis and pulling out their weapons in a standoff. Also seeing Aranea jump off a building and land on Noctis's ship to face off against Noctis in the air in such a true FF dragoon fashion/way was also so badass. Watching those early trailers now is just so intriguing and makes the loss feel even worse. We were genuinely robbed 😭. 

Especially for Nomura that guy was robbed the most. I feel pretty bad for him as he seemed to be pushed out and scapegoated during and after development when he was really passionate about Versus 13 and Noctis and saw him/it as like his second son next to Sora from Kingdom Hearts. Kingdom Hearts was originally gonna have some ties and parallels with Versus especially its names and even DNA and just the way a lot of FF characters are integrated into the story of KH. Today Nomura directly references Versus 13 in Kingdom Hearts 3 with the secret endings and trailers of Verum Rex esp in the Remind dlc and just the whole character of Yozora and his world leading to Kingdom Hearts 4. Also just with the way the gameplay of Versus 13 was gonna be similar to Kingdom Hearts in the early gameplay trailer. Versus 13 was also suggested to be a trilogy and it seems Nomura took that idea and is implementing it in the FF7 Remakes. Versus 13 was also gonna be connected to FF13 and FF Type 0 (Agito) through the connected universe Fabula Nova Crystalis that got scrapped. Noctis and Lightning already parallel each other in their names and aesthetics. It's all just such a big missed/wasted opportunity 😔. 

Then even when Hajime Tabata took over, after 8 years of development hell with Nomura's Versus being scrapped, he essentially had 2 years to make FF15 with those concepts. Understandably Tabata's own vision of 15 which came out pretty differently from Nomura's was also just never fully realized as well. A lot of the content and story was split into a movie, anime, and later dlcs. On top of that there is just generally a lot of content that was cut and even dlcs that never released. There's also so many videos you can find where you see areas that were cut from the game, or just not fully used, and just even more cut content left in the game. The quote in the 2011 trailer "The figure that still lies asleep in the Fantasy" is actually just so ironic now 🥀. 20 years later people still share the same sentiment making videos and forums discussing about what could've been and just the unmatched potential they felt this game had. I'm really curious to see what comes of Nomura's Kingdom Hearts 4 though especially with how it heavily it referenced Versus 13 and just how that will all unfold with Yozora and his world🙏.

Underrated Final Fantasy game, especially by players. 

Pros are: 

* Very good story 
* Fantastic OST
* Satisfying combat and difficulty 
* Broship between the main characters
* Gorgeous graphics

Cons: 

* The story, despite it being very good, isn't told well and requires you to watch a 1h long anime and a 2h long movie to fully understand, plus another bunch of extras that are scattered around the internet. All this extra content should've been included into the game to begin with.
* Performance isn't the best, it is well optimized but the game is still extremely demanding, probably TOO demanding. With an SSD, a 980 ti, 8GB RAM and a 2600k I run it at 50 fps and high preset, but sometimes there's massive stuttering, apparently caused by the game using all my RAM and switching to the pagefile.
* Questing is pretty bad, all the secondary quests seem to be fetch quests, the kind that is like "go here, kill 3 of these and come back", or "go here, collect item and come back". Boring and repetitive.
* Enemy level disparity, you're just driving around a starting lvl 10 area and you get ambushed by a lvl 42 red giant that one-shots your entire party, not fun and not good game design. This stops being a problem when your entire party reaches lvl 50-ish, but still.
* Random encounters are too frequent, imperial troopers rain on you relentlessly while you're trying to do anything in the open world, you kill an entire squad of imperials only for a fresh new one to drop on your location again, almost inmediately. Super annoying.
* Camera can be very clunky sometimes, especially with bushes and trees around there's times when you can't see shit and are forced to warp away from that place just to be able to see anything at all.
* Auto-dodge (holding X) sometimes doesn't work (?), blinking seems to work everytime (pressing X at the last second) but the auto-dodge sometimes doesn't do shit, you hold X and still take attacks to the face instead of automatically phasing, which is what should happen.


The game isn't a 10/10, but it's easily an 8/10 and still very worth playing despite its flaws. It's addictive and overall very fun.

You follow path of Noctis and his friends, you constantly getting yourself into problems, or some would say “ adventures “, and growing as a persons. Definitely recommend finishing bros episodes, since it opens their personalities even more. About Ardyn episode, well, you should do it, no I mean you SHOULD do it and finish it, it will open many truths, specially about true villain of the story.

Speaking about Comrades, the multiplayer expansion, well, as fun it was.. it`s dead, well technically as far as I know servers are up, but its impossible to connect to anyone( at least for me ), we tried with a friend and we got constantly disconnected from each other and randoms are basically non existent. Other then that, it was fun, combat felt a bit better then Noctis one. ( Yes you can play and finish it as offline as well. )

Overall my recommendation would be finish the main story, then finish episodes and comrades and only then attempt New Game+.
